content.summary_of_the_paper: The computation cost of non-autoregressive generation is high especially when the sequence is long. The paper proposes to combine MLP with attention mechanism to get both considerable performance and speed. Specifically, they use the techniques of dimension reduction and covariance matrices computation. Experiments are conducted on Text2Speech, Machine Translation, and Super Resolution tasks. The proposed method speeds up the computation, and can achieve similar performance with autoregressive models.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
+ Significant improvement on reducing computing time and memory usage especially when generating long sequences compared to autoregressive models.
+ Performance is validated on different datasets, including both NLP and CV areas.
+ The effect of hyperparameters is examined in the ablation study.


Cons:
- The equations are mainly approximation, i.e., AMLP(Q; K, V) ≈ f(Q; K, V) and f(Q; K, V) ≈ Attn(Q, K, V). Hence, there is not enough theorical evidence to show whether AMLP integrates the functionality of attention mechanism. And there is not enough support to the claim of “We believe that the matrix QΣK can also be treated as a low-rank matrix.”
- The speed evaluation (Fig. 3) lacks comparison with other linear complexity methods like XCA (Ali et al., 2021).
- The analysis of complexity is a bit confusing: the complexity of NAR with vanilla softmax is supposed to be O(nm). Can the authors explain more on the O((n+m)^2) complexity?
- The performance drop in MT task.

content.title: Response to Review GAYL
content.comment:
Continue the pervious problems

> Q7. The paper needs further polishing

Our reply: Thanks for pointing out our writing problems. We fully take your advice and change the typo as well as confusing parts in our revised paper.

> Q8. The dimension reduction contributes to (Xiong et al., 2021), and the co-variance matrices computation is inspired from (Ali et al., 2021). Considering the two papers, the authors are applying the ideas to NAG area. Hence the novelty is limited.

Our reply: The novelty of our work has mainly three aspects. 
1. From the perspective of problem novelty, our paper is motivated by solving the inefficiency in both time and memory when NAR models process long sequences. Previous NAR generation models suffer from heavy memory costs in inference stage and quadratic time complexity due to quadratic vanilla attention. To reduce the complexity of NAR models from quadratic to linear, we propose AMLP to model both self-attention and cross-attention and produce a linear NAR model. 
2. On the view of technical innovation,  AMLP uses the same concept of low-rank matrices [1, 2, 3, 4] and covariance [5], but models the whole attention  in another way to successfully do cross-attention tasks. 
   1.  Unlike other work (Xiong et al., 2021) that decomposes the softmax matrix, we directly decompose the the $\Sigma$ without any low-rank assumption. We adopt low-rank concept when remaining only max $c$ eigenvalues of $\Sigma$.  
   2. Unlike XCA (Ali et al., 2021) that directly uses cross-covariance to model $QK^\top$, we separately model $Q$ and $K$ with covariance and the cross covariance between $K$ and $V$. Thanks to separate modeling, our AMLP outperforms other MLP-like models in both self-attention and cross-attention.   
   3. In both (Xiong et al., 2021) and  (Ali et al., 2021), they could only replace self-attention and cannot do cross-attention. This strictly restricts that their models cannot be applied in mainstream generation tasks, where alignment between source and target sequences is required. In contrast, AMLP can do cross attention well, which is empirically verified in Table 4.    
3. Our work also builds the connection between MLP and attentive models through the introduction of $\Sigma$. To the best of our knowledge, AMLP is a strong MLP-like architecture that can do cross-attention and hence able to be applied in non-autoregressive generation tasks and feature alignment scenarios.
   
[1] Krzysztof Marcin Choromanski, Valerii Likhosherstov, David Dohan, Xingyou Song, Andreea Gane, Tamas Sarlos, Peter Hawkins, Jared Quincy Davis, Afroz Mohiuddin, Lukasz Kaiser, David Benjamin Belanger, Lucy J Colwell, and Adrian Weller. Rethinking attention with performers. In International Conference on Learning Representations, 2021. URL https://openreview.net/forum?id=Ua6zuk0WRH.   
[2] Yunyang Xiong, Zhanpeng Zeng, Rudrasis Chakraborty, Mingxing Tan, Glenn Fung, Yin Li, and Vikas Singh. Nystromformer: A nystr ¨ om-based algorithm for approximating self-attention. ¨ Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence, 35(16):14138–14148, May 2021. doi: 10.1609/aaai.v35i16.17664. URL https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/17664  
[3] Zhen Qin, Weixuan Sun, Hui Deng, Dongxu Li, Yunshen Wei, Baohong Lv, Junjie Yan, Lingpeng Kong, and Yiran Zhong. cosformer: Rethinking softmax in attention. In International Conference on Learning Representations, 2022. URL https://openreview.net/forum?id=Bl8CQrx2Up4  
[4] Lin Zheng, Chong Wang, and Lingpeng Kong. Linear complexity randomized self-attention mechanism. arXiv preprint arXiv:2204.04667, 2022.  
[5] Alaaeldin Ali, Hugo Touvron, Mathilde Caron, Piotr Bojanowski, Matthijs Douze, Armand Joulin, Ivan Laptev, Natalia Neverova, Gabriel Synnaeve, Jakob Verbeek, et al. Xcit: Cross-covariance image transformers. Advances in neural information processing systems, 34:20014–20027, 2021.

content.title: Response to Review GAYL
content.comment:
Thanks for your helpful comments and detailed suggestions for our paper! We update the revised paper and respond to your questions below:

> Q1. "The equations are mainly approximation, i.e., AMLP(Q; K, V) ≈ f(Q; K, V) and f(Q; K, V) ≈ Attn(Q, K, V). Hence, there is not enough theoretical evidence to show whether AMLP integrates the functionality of attention mechanism." and  "And there is not enough support to the claim of “We believe that the matrix QΣK can also be treated as a low-rank matrix.”

Our reply: AMLP's philosophy is not from approximation but kernel function and low rank decomposition. We here show that AMLP fuses attentive ability through kernel function approximation, matrix decomposition and reformulation. We will also add the following explanation to our revised paper.
  1. In vanilla attention, $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top)$ is a softmax kernel which can be decomposed into a multiplication of two kernel functions: $\phi(Q)\cdot\phi(K)^\top$, which is verified in Performer [1], cosFormer [3] and LARA [4]. Hence, we here use a distance matrix $\Sigma$ to serve as a bridge which enables $Q\Sigma K^\top$ to be decomposed with fewer eigenspectrums like Performer.
  2.  The low rank approximation of the attention matrix, $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top)$,  does not impact the performance much, which is verified by Nystromformer [2]. Based on their findings, the kernel function $Q\Sigma K^\top$, which is an approximation of the softmax kernel, can also enjoy lower computation costs from low rank approximation.
  3. Combined with two results, AMLP reformulates the attention $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top)$ with $Q\Sigma K^\top$ and uses Nystrom's findings to decompose $\Sigma$ into two matrices while reducing eigenspectrums. Finally, AMLP reparameterizes the decomposed matrices and maintains the attentive functionality as Attn(Q, K, V).


> Q2. The speed evaluation (Fig. 3) lacks comparison with other linear complexity methods like XCA (Ali et al., 2021).

Our reply: we replenish the comparison against XCA and gMLP in TTS task below and the revised paper:

  |  Arch | MCD | Inference time (s) | Speed-up | 
  | ---- | ---- | ---- |  ---- |
  |  Vanilla | 3.4748 | 212.781 | 1.00x | 
  |  gMLP | 3.4025 |  187.379 | 1.14x  |
  |  XCA | 3.5003 | 186.382 | 1.14x |
  | AMLP |  3.3274 | 188.743 | 1.13x | 

The reason why we do not add them in Fig. 3 is that the synthetic experiment consists of a transformer decoder. In the decoder, gMLP and XCA can only replace self attention, which cannot produce a linear decoder model. 

> Q3. Can the authors explain more on the O((n+m)^2) complexity?

Our reply: We analyze the whole encoder-decoder architecture. 
  1. In the encoder, vanilla attention costs $O(m^2)$; 
  2. In the decoder, vanilla attention costs $O(n^2)$ for self attention and $O(nm)$ for cross attention. Thus the total time complexity is $O(n^2+nm+m^2)$, which equals to $O((n+m)^2)$ in big O annotation. 
  3. However, we also admit that it may bring some confusion, so we change it back to $O(n^2+m^2+nm)$ in our revised paper.
   
> Q4. The performance drop in MT task.

Our reply: We admit that there exists performance drop for existing efficient attention mechanisms. We  replace all vanilla attention in an encoder-decoder model to fuse AMLP with NAR translation model. This produces a linear model to tradeoff between performance and efficiency.  We are also exploring better AMLP variants to bridge the gap between AMLP and vanilla attention.

> Q5. Is f(Q; K, V) an approximation of Attn(Q, K, V)

Our reply: Yes. AMLP is motivated from the approximation of Attn(Q, K, V), which is denoted as f(Q; K, V), but its actual design is a reformulation and reparameterization of Attn(Q, K, V). Combined with the kernel approximation from [1, 3, 4] and low rank decomposition[2], AMLP reformulates the attention $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top)$ with $Q\Sigma K^\top$ and uses Nystrom's findings to decompose $\Sigma$ into two matrices. Finally, AMLP reparameterizes the decomposed matrices and maintains the attentive functionality as Attn(Q, K, V). Therefore, the final form of AMLP is not an approximation of Attn(Q, K, V). 


> Q6. According to Eq. (7), must W_{Q, K, V} be W_{Q, K}^TK^T

Our reply: $W_{Q, K, V}$ here is another weight matrix computed from $Q, K, V$, instead of a product from $W_{Q,K}$ and $K$. 
The computation of $W_{Q,K,V}$ is illustrated in Eq. 10 and Eq. 12. Basically, $W_{Q, K, V}$ is computed from $W_{Q, K}$ and $K, V$,    

$$
W_{\mathbf{Q,K,V}}=\mathbf{L}^\top\sigma_2(\mathbf{K}^\top \mathbf{V})
$$

$$
W_{\\mathbf{Q,K,V}}=\\sigma_2(\\mathbf{L^\\top K^\\top) V}
$$

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work presents a Transformer MLP alternative, AMLP (Attentive Multi-Layer Perceptron). A Transformer model with AMLP has linear time and space complexity. The paper also shows that AMLP in an NAR Transformer is effective: it yields competitive performance in NAR and other benchmarks, and it has excellent efficiency compared with other low-rank Transformers such as Performer.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths

1. The proposed AMLP architecture is a novel low-rank module that can be applied in Transformer sequence models. It has linear time and space efficiency. The illustration of the AMLP module in Figure 1 is very clear and easy to understand.

2. The paper includes comparisons of AMLP with various low-rank Transformer architectures in a wide variety of tasks, including text-to-speech, non-autoregressive translation, and even image super-resolution. In most experiments presented in the paper, AMLP has very competitive performance compared with other models.

## Weaknesses

1. The efficiency between local, gMLP, XCA, ABC, AMLP are not compared in this work. For example, how much times slower is AMLP compared with "local" when the sequence length is 512 (the most typical sequence length in most applications), and the same for gMLP, XCA, and ABC.

2. It would be better to also **show the performance of AMLP in auto-regressive (AR) translation in Table 2** . According to the formulation of AMLP, this method is not designed to utilize anything specific or limited to non-autoregressive translation. Therefore, it is supposed to work well in AR translation too. If the results in AR translation is also good, it would be greater contribution. However, if the results in AR translation is not so good, the result should also be shown in the paper and preferably more detailed analysis on why AMLP does not work for AR translation.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The clarity, quality of this paper is good. The paper is missing a reproducibility statement section. The code is not released in this version of paper and it is impossible to reproduce the results at the current stage, but the author promises to release the code in the future.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work proposes a novel formulation of low-rank attention module to be used in Transformers, and this work shows strong empirical results of AMLP in multiple benchmarks in NLP and computer graphics. However, several important experiments are still missing and these missing experiments are crucial in evaluating the contribution of this paper. So I would give a marginal rejection recommendation and I would be happy to increase my review scores if the relevant results are added.

content.title: Response to Review w1ve
content.comment:
Thanks for your helpful comments and detailed suggestions for our paper! We update the revised paper and respond to your questions below:

> Q1. The efficiency between local, gMLP, XCA, ABC, AMLP are not compared in this work. 

Our reply: We do execute efficiency comparison in Fig 2, where we compare AMLP with ABC and local in TTS tasks. TTS tasks involve sequences with an average length 559, which is a general sequence length in most scenarios. We also replenish the comparison between AMLP and gMLP and XCA below and and we will add these results in our Fig. 2 in the revision paper. In this experiment, we run each model at their inference stages 5 times at the same GPU and average time costs on these 5 runs to reduce noise.

  |  Arch | MCD | Inference time (s) | Speed-up | 
  | ---- | ---- | ---- |  ---- |
  |  Vanilla | 3.4748 | 212.781 | 1.00x | 
  |  gMLP | 3.4025 |  187.379 | 1.14x  |
  |  XCA | 3.5003 | 186.382 | 1.14x |
  | AMLP |  3.3274 | 188.743 | 1.13x | 

> Q2. It would be better to also show the performance of AMLP in auto-regressive (AR) translation in Table 2 .

Our reply: AMLP is not straightforward to be applied to the decoder of AR models with high efficiency. We here add the results that AMLP is applied in transformer encoder:

  |  Arch | WMT' 14 en-de | WMT' 14 de-en | 
  | ---- | ---- | ---- |  
  |  Transformer | 27.38 | 31.26 | 
  |  Transformer-AMLP | 26.24 | 29.77 | 

The reason why we do not apply AMLP in transformer decoder is that we should handle the causality problem. We add further explanation here and our revision paper.
  1. In AR models, the self/cross attention is different from NAR models and they require to maintain causality due to teacher forcing training. To enable causal AMLP, the overall time consumption and memory costs in training phase are hugely increased. Such drawback is also revealed in most efficient attention (like Nystromformer, Local, cosFormer, Performer) that also adopt softmax kernel decomposition for speed-up. To replace decoder self attention, they also need to pay extra complexity during training, which is discussed with detail in Appendix A. Therefore, AMLP is also not straightforward to be adopted for AR models. 
  2. In contrast to AR models where typical efficient models and AMLP all suffer from inefficiency, the training objective and i.i.d. assumption of NAR models avoid teacher forcing and thus suit application of efficient attention and AMLP. As a result, AMLP is dedicated to NAR models for even higher efficiency in both training and inference.
  3. We take AMLP-cov as an example to show why causal AMLP would increase training costs.  
Given a query token $\\boldsymbol{q}_t$, the covariance $\\mathbf{S}_t^{\\mathbf{Q}}$ and $\\mathbf{S}_t^{\\mathbf{K}}$ of $\\mathbf{K}_t$ and $\\mathbf{Q}_t$, and the cross-covariance $\\mathbf{z}_t$ of $\\mathbf{K}_t$ and $\\mathbf{V}_t$,  
the weight matrices 
 $W\_{ \mathbf{Q,K} } $ and $W_\mathbf{{\mathbf{Q,K,V}}}$ are formulated as follows:

$$  
W_{\\mathbf{Q}_{t},\\mathbf{K}_t}=\\mathbf{L}_t^\\top=C_q(\\sigma_2(\\mathbf{S}_t^{\\mathbf{Q}}))+C_k(\\sigma_2(\\mathbf{S}_t^{\\mathbf{K}})) 
$$

$$
W_{\\mathbf{Q}_{t},\\mathbf{K}_t, \\mathbf{V}_t}=\\mathbf{L}_t^\\top\\sigma_2(\\mathbf{z}_t)  
$$

where $\\mathbf{S}\_t^{\\mathbf{Q}}=\\mathbf{S}_{t-1}^{\\mathbf{Q}}+\\boldsymbol{q}_t^\\top\\boldsymbol{q}_t$, $\\mathbf{S}_t^{\\mathbf{K}}=\\mathbf{S}\_{t-1}^{\\mathbf{K}}+\\boldsymbol{k}_t^\\top\\boldsymbol{k}_t$ and $\\mathbf{z}_t=\\mathbf{z}\_{t-1}+\\boldsymbol{k}_t^\\top\\boldsymbol{v}_t$.
These computation steps increase heavy memory costs and large time consumption in the training phase, with an additional $O(ncd)$ costs beyond the overall computation.

> Q3. The paper is missing a reproducibility statement section. The code is not released in this version of paper and it is impossible to reproduce the results at the current stage, but the author promises to release the code in the future.  

Our reply: To follow the "double blinded" rule, we do not release the actual codebase in the submitted paper. We add AMLP's codes in the supplementary materials.

content.title: Response to Review eR9D
content.comment:
Continue the previous problems

> Q3. The efficiency analysis does not have enough results. Given that efficiency is a main motivation of this is paper, I'd expect more detailed evidence on efficiency improvement reported for both training and inference.

Our reply: Our efficiency analysis contains two parts: NAR-AMLP reduces time costs and memory costs in long sequence settings and AMLP obtains good performance-efficiency tradeoff in usual sequence length setting (559) in speech synthesis. 
  1. we demonstrate our AMLP's efficiency when the sequence length is scaled up from 256 to 8192 in Fig 3. Although AMLP's efficiency is lower than vanilla attention when sequence is relatively short, it shows great efficiency gain when the sequence becomes longer than 1024. 
  2. Meanwhile, AMLP is proposed to mitigate the memory inefficiency of NAR models at inference stage and the time inefficiency of NAR models at training phase in long sequence modeling settings, which is also presented in Fig 3.
  3. (speech synthesis results; authentic experiments)Apart from synthesis experiment, we also compare AMLP with other efficient models at authentic experiments, TTS task. We present the performance-efficiency tradeoff of each efficient attention as well as AMLP in Fig. 2. The results of gMLP and XCA in Fig. 2 are omitted and we replenish the comparison below and we will replenish the figure in our revision paper.  
    
  |  Arch | MCD | Inference time (s) | Speed-up | 
  | ---- | ---- | ---- |  ---- |
  |  Vanilla | 3.4748 | 212.781 | 1.00x | 
  |  gMLP | 3.4025 |  187.379 | 1.14x  |
  |  XCA | 3.5003 | 186.382 | 1.14x |
  | AMLP |  3.3274 | 188.743 | 1.13x |  

> Q4. local and ABC has larger drop in NAR than AR

Our reply: In typical encoder-decoder transformer models, there exist an encoder self attention, a decoder self attention and a decoder cross attention. In NAR models, the decoder self attention is the same with encoder self attention. Based on this setting, the performance drops of ABC/local in NAR models result from different reasons:
- ABC:  There is a low correlation between performances of a certain attention in encoders and decoders. In NAR models, the decoder self attention is noncausal while it is causal in AR models. Therefore, the performance of NAR models is highly related to the capability of noncausal self attention (also known as encoder self attention) instead of causal self attention (also known as decoder self attention).  ABC's noncausal self attention ability is much lower than vanilla attention, which has been empirically verified in our Table 3. Thus its performance drop in NAR models is much higher than applied in AR models. 
- Local: Local Attention is powerful at AR models for teacher forcing property of decoder self attention. This teacher forcing property not only brings more condition signals for generation, but also brings strong position alignment for Local attention. However, in NAR models, such teacher forcing information and position alignment information are both lost and models that have strong global modeling ability can keep a high performance. In contrast, local attention with a small window size (5 in MT setting) loses the global modeling ability. A larger window size for local attention may mitigate this drawback, but its efficiency will also be lowered greatly.

> Q5. How was the speed-up measured in Figure 2?

Our reply: we run each model at their inference stages 5 times at the same GPU and average time costs on these 5 runs to reduce noise.

content.comment:
Thanks for your extremely valuable comments and feedback. We respond to your questions below. We also update the revised paper.

> Q1. Since the goal of AMLP is to improve the efficiency of long sequence generation, evaluation on document-level MT tasks would be more appropriate than the chosen WMT en-de benchmarks.

Our reply: Document-level MT is exactly more suitable than MT task while now the non-autoregressive generation (NAR) models are yet not investigated enough to be applied in document translation. In other words, to the best of our knowledge, no appropriate NAR baselines are available in document translation. We are exploring efficient NAR document-level MT models in our future work.

> Q2. Although the focus of this paper is NAR, for completeness AMLP should also be compared to local and ABC in the AR case in Table 2.

Our reply: As is explained above, AMLP is not straightforward to be applied to the decoder of AR models with high efficiency. We here add the results that AMLP is applied in transformer encoder:

  |  Arch | WMT' 14 en-de | WMT' 14 de-en | 
  | ---- | ---- | ---- |  
  |  Transformer | 27.38 | 31.26 | 
  |  Transformer-AMLP | 26.24 | 29.77 | 

The reason why we do not apply AMLP in transformer decoder is that we should handle the causality problem.  We add detailed explanation below and our revision paper.
  1. In AR models, the self/cross attention is different from NAR models and they require to maintain causality due to teacher forcing training. To enable causal (decoder) AMLP, the overall time consumption and memory costs in training phase are hugely increased. Such drawback is also revealed in  most efficient attention (like Nystromformer, Local, cosFormer, Performer) that also adopt softmax kernel decomposition for speed-up. To replace decoder self attention, they also need to pay extra complexity during training. Therefore, these efficient attention and AMLP are also not straightforward to be adopted for AR models. 
  2. In contrast to AR models where typical efficient models and AMLP all suffer from inefficiency, the training objective and identically independent distribution (i.i.d.) assumption of NAR models avoid teacher forcing and thus suit application of efficient attention and AMLP. As a result, AMLP is dedicated to NAR models for even higher efficiency in both training and inference.
  3. We take AMLP-cov as an example to show why causal AMLP would increase training costs.

Given a query token $\\boldsymbol{q}_t$, the covariance $\\mathbf{S}_t^{\\mathbf{Q}}$ and $\\mathbf{S}_t^{\\mathbf{K}}$ of $\\mathbf{K}_t$ and $\\mathbf{Q}_t$, and the cross-covariance $\\mathbf{z}_t$ of $\\mathbf{K}_t$ and $\\mathbf{V}_t$,  
the weight matrices 
 $W\_{ \mathbf{Q,K} } $ and $W_\mathbf{{\mathbf{Q,K,V}}}$ are formulated as follows:

$$  
W_{\\mathbf{Q}_{t},\\mathbf{K}_t}=\\mathbf{L}_t^\\top=C_q(\\sigma_2(\\mathbf{S}_t^{\\mathbf{Q}}))+C_k(\\sigma_2(\\mathbf{S}_t^{\\mathbf{K}})) 
$$

$$
W_{\\mathbf{Q}_{t},\\mathbf{K}_t, \\mathbf{V}_t}=\\mathbf{L}_t^\\top\\sigma_2(\\mathbf{z}_t)  
$$

where $\\mathbf{S}\_t^{\\mathbf{Q}}=\\mathbf{S}_{t-1}^{\\mathbf{Q}}+\\boldsymbol{q}_t^\\top\\boldsymbol{q}_t$, $\\mathbf{S}_t^{\\mathbf{K}}=\\mathbf{S}\_{t-1}^{\\mathbf{K}}+\\boldsymbol{k}_t^\\top\\boldsymbol{k}_t$ and $\\mathbf{z}_t=\\mathbf{z}\_{t-1}+\\boldsymbol{k}_t^\\top\\boldsymbol{v}_t$.
These computation steps increase heavy memory costs and large time consumption in the training phase, with an additional $O(ncd)$ costs beyond the overall computation.
